newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Talks over Vietnam oil refinery hit problems again.
newsitem.headline: Talks over Vietnam oil refinery hit problems again.

text.p: Vietnam's plans for its first oil refinery appeared to have run into problems again on Thursday as wide differences emerged between Hanoi and prospective partners, but a senior official said a deal was still being sought.
Ho Si Thoang, of state oil firm Petrovietnam, told Reuters that Hanoi was not prepared to offer the concessions being demanded in talks by the foreign partners.
But he denied reports that talks over the future of the $1.4 Dung Quat billion refinery project had broken down.

"We have informed them that the government cannot accept any changes in the guidelines, so if they will follow the project with Petrovietnam it will be very good, but if not we need to find a way to continue the project," he said by phone.
Petrovietnam's partners in the project include Taiwan's Chinese Petroleum Corp, South Korea's LG Group, Stone & Webster, Malaysia's Petronas and U.S.-based Conoco.

They replaced French oil firm Total SA which pulled out in 1995 branding the project economically unviable because of the remote location -- 1,000 km (600 miles) north of the country's main oilfields and consumption base.

In recent months, however, negotiations with the new consortium have slowed, reportedly because of demands that Hanoi give price guarantees for the refined petroleum, and over demands for access to the domestic consumer market.
Thoang reiterated Petrovietnam's position that Vietnam was prepared go ahead with the project alone if no deal was reached, despite the costs.
However, a spokeswoman for Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Thursday her company was not prepared to back down.
"We have submitted our proposal (to the Vietnamese government), but if it cannot commit to our requirements, we will not do it," she told Reuters.
A senior Conoco official was quoted in similar vein earlier this week as saying that unless Vietnam changed its mind about the location then the U.S.-based firm would also pull out.
Thoang said a change of location was out of the question.

"The Dung Quat area must be developed. The site location is not a very important role (factor) in this project," he said. "The refinery industry now is not very profitable. It's not an issue of Dung Quat."
